notes: TUPE assignment test for a long-serving trade union steward; permission refused with no realistic prospect of success.

enrichment.short_title: TUPE transfer and union steward assignment

statutes_considered.title: Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981

key_facts: Birmingham City Council transferred housing repairs contracts A and B to Serviceteam Birmingham Ltd under TUPE.
Mr Gaston, employed since 1969, had worked for over 20 years as a full-time AEEU chief federation steward rather than as an operative plumber.
The employment tribunal found he was not assigned to the undertaking transferred to Serviceteam and had remained a council employee.
The council sought permission to appeal, arguing estoppel, inadequate reasons, and that he was employed as a plumber.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal's dismissal of the council's appeal against an employment tribunal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; the EAT's conclusion that Mr Gaston was not assigned to the transferred undertaking was the only possible answer on the facts.
enrichment.ratio: The TUPE test is whether an employee was assigned to the undertaking or part of the undertaking transferred, not whether he was nominally employed as a plumber; a functional investigation of the employee's role at transfer is required and nominal job titles are misleading where the employee had not worked as part of the contract teams for decades.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Gaston was assigned to the contracts A and B undertaking for TUPE purposes
Whether estoppel arose from an earlier employment tribunal decision describing him as a plumber
Whether the employment tribunal's decision was inadequately reasoned or wrong
linked_authorities: Arie Botzen v Rotterdamsche Droogdok Maatschappij [1985] ECR 519

confidence.notes: Single-judge permission judgment with clear TUPE test and factual findings; estoppel and reasoning grounds are briefly addressed.

notes: Landmark TAG/Claims Direct costs appeal on section 29 ATE premium assessment and AIL referral fee; Senior Costs Judge upheld in full.

enrichment.short_title: Accident Group ATE insurance premium recoverability under section 29
key_facts: The Accident Group Ltd operated a claims management scheme providing after-the-event insurance and bank loans to personal injury claimants.
Claimants in test cases sought recovery from defendants of TAG premiums under section 29 of the Access to Justice Act 1999.
Senior Costs Judge Hurst used a deconstructionist approach, starting with sums paid to underwriters and deducting non-qualifying elements.
The court upheld findings that the AIL investigation fee was an unlawful referral fee and not a recoverable disbursement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from detailed costs assessments before the Senior Costs Judge in TAG scheme test cases.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; the Senior Costs Judge's premium calculations, LEAP rejection, £30 insurance services allowance, and AIL fee ruling were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A section 29 premium is the sum paid to the insurer, not the fee charged by an intermediary for a basket of services; where part of a block fee is a disguised referral fee paid to a sister company of the introducer, it is irrecoverable and cannot form part of the qualifying premium.
legal_issues: Whether TAG premiums qualifying under section 29 should be assessed from client payments or underwriter premiums
Whether LEAP payments could be added to 2000 premiums
Whether cost of insurance services beyond £30 was recoverable
Whether the AIL fee was a referral fee or recoverable disbursement
linked_authorities: Callery v Gray (No 2) [2001] 1 WLR 2142
Claims Direct [2003] EWCA Civ 136
Halloran v Delaney [2003] 1 WLR 28

confidence.notes: Long judgment with detailed scheme analysis and clear outcomes on premium methodology and AIL fee; test-case context is explicit.

notes: Charging order nullity argument rejected; litigants in person directed to use section 3(5) Charging Orders Act or CPR variation routes.

enrichment.short_title: Charging orders over development land not nullities
key_facts: Mr Nelson contracted to buy Plot 9 from Greening but failed to complete; prolonged litigation led to specific performance and accumulated costs of about £80,000.
Peter Smith J executed a transfer to Mr Nelson, registered it through Greening, and granted a charging order securing Greening's costs.
Miss Hanley and Mr Nelson applied to Lindsay J and Lewison J to set aside those orders as nullities rather than appealing them.
Both judges dismissed the applications, holding the orders were valid though subject to discharge or variation under statute or the CPR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal against refusals to set aside charging and transfer orders as nullities.
enrichment.outcome: Applications dismissed with costs assessed at £1,864; permission to appeal refused on the basis that the nullity argument was bound to fail.
enrichment.ratio: A charging order properly made is not a nullity because of procedural defects or because a third party was not formally joined; the correct route is appeal or an application under section 3(5) of the Charging Orders Act 1979 or the CPR to vary or discharge the order.
legal_issues: Whether Peter Smith J's charging and transfer orders were nullities
Whether Miss Hanley could challenge orders despite not being a party
Whether Lindsay J and Lewison J should have dealt with CPR set-aside grounds

confidence.notes: Procedural outcome is clear though the underlying land dispute history is complex; merits of the charging orders were not decided.

notes: VAT partial exemption appeal on BLP direct and immediate link test; marketing input tax apportioned to exempt insurance intermediary services.

enrichment.short_title: VAT apportionment of mobile phone advertising input tax
key_facts: Dial-a-Phone marketed mobile phones and arranged Cornhill insurance, earning commission on premiums after a three-month free period.
It spent about £1 million per month on advertising and claimed full deduction of input VAT on marketing services.
Customs ruled the input tax was residual because advertising was directly linked to both taxable phone sales and exempt insurance intermediary services.
The VAT tribunal and Blackburne J upheld partial apportionment under regulation 101(2)(d).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from the High Court dismissing an appeal against a VAT and Duties Tribunal decision on input tax attribution.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs of £7,842.50; marketing and advertising input tax was correctly treated as residual tax attributable to both taxable and exempt supplies.
enrichment.ratio: Under the BLP direct and immediate link test, input tax on marketing may be apportioned where advertising promotes a package including exempt insurance intermediary services supplied to Cornhill for consideration under the Heads of Agreement, even if taxable mobile phone sales are commercially primary.
legal_issues: Whether marketing input tax was attributable exclusively to taxable supplies
Whether insurance intermediary services were supplied for consideration when customers might never pay premiums
Whether the tribunal misapplied BLP by looking at ultimate aim or timing
Whether Note (7) to Schedule 9 excluded a direct link
index_terms: BLP Group plc v Customs & Excise
linked_authorities: BLP Group plc v Customs & Excise Commissioners (Case C-4/94) [1995] STC 424
Midland Bank plc v Customs & Excise Commissioners (Case C-98/98) [2000] STC 501
Customs & Excise Commissioners v Southern Primary Housing Association Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 1662

confidence.notes: Undisputed facts and detailed VAT authority analysis; outcome and BLP test application are explicit throughout.

notes: Section 5A Sex Offenders Act restraining order appeal reconciling Beaney and Halloren; order on counts 1-7 quashed and terms narrowed.

enrichment.short_title: Sex offender internet restraining order terms and duration

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: A former teacher pleaded guilty to making and possessing indecent images of children spanning 1984 to 2002, including altered photographs of pupils.
The judge imposed concurrent sentences and an indefinite section 5A restraining order prohibiting any personal computer or internet access except at lawful employment.
The appeal concerned only the restraining order, adjourned because of tension between R v Halloren and R v Beaney.
Section 5A applied only to possession counts 8-24 as it came into force on 2 May 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a section 5A Sex Offenders Act restraining order imposed at sentence in the Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; restraining order on counts 1-7 quashed, and the order on counts 8-24 varied to prohibit downloading from the internet except for lawful employment or study.
enrichment.ratio: A section 5A order requires necessity to protect the public from death or serious personal injury through further sexual offences; downloading indecent images contributes to harm to depicted children, but the order must be proportionate and not oppressively bar all legitimate internet use by the offender's household.
legal_issues: Whether there was material justifying a section 5A restraining order
Whether an indefinite order was appropriate
Whether the prohibition on owning or using any computer with internet access was too wide
linked_authorities: R v Halloren [2004] EWCA Crim 233
R v Beaney [2004] EWCA Crim 449

confidence.notes: Short criminal judgment with clear statutory analysis and varied order terms; sentence itself was not appealed.

notes: Family partnership property dispute; draft declaration of trust and recorded telephone call undermined appellants' case on Big House and Barking Road assets.

enrichment.short_title: Fine Fabrics family partnership beneficial ownership dispute
key_facts: The Shah brothers carried on the Fine Fabrics drapery partnership; three brothers died leaving estates claiming one-sixth shares in partnership properties.
Claimant Sangeeta Mehra argued only the six brothers were partners and that the Big House and Barking Road properties were partnership assets.
Defendants contended all twelve siblings were partners or held constructive trusts, and that certain properties were held outside the partnership.
A draft 2000 declaration of trust listing partnership properties and a recorded 2001 telephone conversation with Ratilal Shah were central evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Chancery Division trial declaring the six-brother partnership and ordering sale of disputed properties.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Big House and Barking Road properties were partnership assets and the sisters' constructive trust claim failed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a draft declaration of trust and contemporaneous admissions show the brothers treated properties as partnership assets to the exclusion of sisters, and sisters' contributions were gifts or loans rather than direct purchase contributions, a constructive trust based on common intention cannot succeed under Lloyds Bank v Rosset principles.
legal_issues: Whether only the six brothers or all twelve siblings were Fine Fabrics partners
Whether the Big House and Barking Road properties were partnership assets
Whether sisters acquired beneficial interests by constructive trust
Whether new evidence from Atul Shah warranted a retrial
linked_authorities: Lloyds Bank plc v Rosset [1991] 1 AC 107

confidence.notes: Detailed factual findings at trial; appeal turned on weight of evidence rather than novel legal principle.

notes: Fourteen meritless litigant-in-person applications dismissed; court proposed extended civil restraint and Attorney-General referral over Perotti saga.

enrichment.short_title: Perotti professional negligence appeals and vexatious litigation
key_facts: Mr Perotti sued Collyer-Bristow for negligence over their brief 1992-1993 retainer in estate administration proceedings concerning his uncle's will.
Lindsay J dismissed the claim after a long trial, refusing permission to appeal; Perotti filed 14 late interlocutory and substantive appeal applications.
The main issues were failure to plead administrator fee and investment management claims in the resettled statement of claim before an unless order deadline.
The court noted Perotti had made about 80 applications since 1997, most refused, and an extended civil restraint order was already in place.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Fourteen applications for permission to appeal against trial rulings and the substantive judgment, plus a transcript funding application.
enrichment.outcome: All 14 applications dismissed as totally devoid of merit; the court proposed varying Neuberger J's extended civil restraint order and referring the matter to the Attorney-General.
enrichment.ratio: Appeal grounds must identify why a decision was wrong under CPR 52.11; repeated meritless applications by a vexatious litigant in person may justify paper-only disposal and enhanced civil restraint to protect court resources.
legal_issues: Whether solicitors were negligent in failing to include administration fee and investment claims in December 1992 pleadings
Whether the retainer was lawfully terminated
Whether trial adjournments and case management rulings were wrongly exercised
What further restraint should apply to future applications
linked_authorities: Nestle v National Westminster Bank plc [1993] 1 WLR 1260
McPhilemy v Times Newspapers Ltd (No 2) [2000] 1 WLR 1732
Bhamjee v Forsdick (No 2)

confidence.notes: Very long judgment but each application and the substantive negligence findings are addressed systematically.

notes: Accountant negligence appeal on CPO rollover relief causation; trial judge entitled to find client would have preferred PPR relief route.

enrichment.short_title: Negligent failure to advise on compulsory purchase rollover relief
key_facts: Fairhursts advised Mr Floyd and his company on tax arising from a 1991 compulsory purchase yielding about £900,000 compensation.
They failed to advise that Mr Floyd could claim CPO rollover relief by reinvesting in qualifying land, causing £156,560 capital gains tax to be paid.
Mr Floyd instead bought Westage Farm and later achieved about £112,018 tax-free gains using principal private residence relief.
The trial judge found on the balance of probabilities Mr Floyd would not have used CPO relief even if advised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a Chancery trial on negligent tax advice, Revenue investigation costs, and accountants' fees.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; no damages for lost CPO relief because causation was not established, with PPR gains set off if liability had arisen.
enrichment.ratio: Where a client would probably have chosen principal private residence relief over compulsory purchase rollover relief, negligent failure to advise on CPO relief does not cause recoverable loss; appellate courts should be reluctant to interfere with a trial judge's evaluation of what a particular client would hypothetically have done.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Floyd would have utilised CPO relief if properly advised
Whether a 25% discount for deferred tax liability was excessive
Whether PPR tax savings should be set off against any CPO loss
Whether the appellants could timely pay tax and whether Revenue settlement benefits should be credited

linked_authorities: Benmax v Austin Motor Co Ltd [1955] AC 370
Assicurazioni Generali SPA v Arab Insurance Group [2003] 1 WLR 577
Johnson v Gore Wood [2002] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Comprehensive judgment on factual review standards and tax mitigation choices; outcomes on each issue are clearly stated.

notes: Major Article 81 beer tie appeal allowed on liability; damages assessed provisionally at about £131,336 using 1993 disposal dates.

enrichment.short_title: Pub beer tie breach of Article 81 EC Treaty
key_facts: Bernard Crehan took tied leases of The Phoenix and The Cock Inn in Staines from Inntrepreneur on condition he buy beer only from the supplier.
His businesses failed and he lost the pubs in 1993; he claimed the beer tie agreements breached Article 81 and sought damages.
Park J dismissed the claim, finding Delimitis market foreclosure conditions were not satisfied.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal on liability and provisionally assessed damages at about £131,336 based on 1993 disposal dates and lease premium multiples.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with respondent's notice from dismissal of an Article 81 damages claim after a long Chancery trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on liability; provisional damages of £131,336 plus interest, with quantum details to be finalised at a further hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Exclusive beer supply ties in the post-1989 pub market could infringe Article 81 where Delimitis conditions on market foreclosure are met; damages for loss of a tied tenancy should be measured at the dates the tenant gave up possession rather than by speculative ten-year projections.
legal_issues: Whether Delimitis condition 1 on market foreclosure was satisfied
Whether the beer ties caused Crehan's business failure
At what date damages for loss of the pubs should be assessed
Whether block exemption or individual exemption applied
linked_authorities: Delimitis v Henninger Bräu AG [1991] ECR I-935
Crehan v Inntrepreneur Pub Co [2003] EuLR 663

confidence.notes: Very long judgment but liability reversal and provisional quantum are clearly stated; some tax and interest points remained open.

notes: Race Relations Act direct discrimination appeal dismissed; housing department glass ceiling finding and assimilation scoring upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Direct race discrimination in local authority housing department
key_facts: Mr Rihal, a Sikh surveyor with a pronounced accent, complained of a racial glass ceiling in Ealing's Housing Department between 1996 and 2000.
He was not promoted when white colleagues with fewer qualifications acted up or were assimilated to senior posts in reorganisations.
Mr Foxall scored Mr Rihal poorly in assimilation exercises and an interview panel gave Mr Gaffikin opportunities Mr Rihal was denied.
Mr Dallison delayed handling Mr Rihal's grievance for over fourteen months.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissing an appeal against race discrimination findings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs of £4,051; direct discrimination upheld on complaints about duty allocation, assimilation, appointment, and grievance handling.
enrichment.ratio: Where a departmental ethnic audit shows a white managerial elite in a diverse borough and an employer cannot explain less favourable treatment of a qualified non-white employee, tribunals may infer racial grounds from the totality of decisions including assimilation scoring and interview conduct without requiring a finding that a white comparator would definitely have succeeded.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal made adequate primary findings before inferring discrimination
Whether assimilation scoring amounted to less favourable treatment on racial grounds
Whether the 1999 interview process was racially discriminatory
Whether delayed grievance handling involved a proper comparator exercise

Qureshi v London Borough of Newham

King v The Great Britain China Centre [1991] IRLR 513
Chapman v Simon [1994] IRLR 273
Anya v University of Oxford [2001] IRLR 371
